props.title: Track of the Moon Beast
props.initialSlug: Scientist turns into deadly were-lizard under moonlight

sections.content: Track of the Moon Beast (1976) stands as a fascinating example of 1970s low-budget creature features, following the unfortunate tale of Paul Carlson, a mineralogist who gets hit by a lunar meteorite and transforms into a lizard monster during full moons. It shares DNA with other transformation horror films like The Wolf Man (1941) and An American Werewolf in London (1981), but with distinctly cheaper production values that place it firmly in the "so bad it's good" category alongside films like Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959).

sections.content: The film's Native American subplot and pseudo-scientific explanations reflect common B-movie tropes of the era, similar to those found in The Giant Gila Monster (1959) and Night of the Blood Beast (1958). The awkward romance, stilted dialogue, and bizarre musical interludes - including the infamous "California Lady" song - make it prime material for comedy commentary shows like Mystery Science Theater 3000 (1988-1999), which famously featured the film. SUBHEAD: Legacy in B-Movie Culture

While Track of the Moon Beast never achieved the cult status of contemporaries like The Incredible Melting Man (1977) or Food of the Gods (1976), it represents a unique snapshot of regional filmmaking in the 1970s. Shot in Albuquerque with local talent, it follows the tradition of independent horror productions like The Legend of Boggy Creek (1972) in attempting to create Hollywood-style monster movies on shoestring budgets.
